title: FIA to introduce full-time stewards in F1 from 2027
excerpt:
The FIA has announced that it will begin recruiting full-time stewards from the 2027 season onwards in order to “bring even greater levels of consistency and dedication to race officiating”.

Stewards are responsible for judging regulation breaches, reviewing on-track incidents and handing out penalties over the course of each race weekend, with four personnel – including a former driver – selected from a larger group.

However, the governing body is now aiming to establish a department of 12-15 full-time individuals, beginning with a phased introduction in which a small number of “experienced international stewards” will complement the existing pool of qualified officials.

The group will then expand for 2028 and beyond to ensure “continuity and expertise within the stewarding structure” and advance fairness in decision-making.

It will also offer a chance to identify areas that require greater clarification, which could subsequently inform regulation changes and support other single-seater series in the future.

Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA, said: “This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport.

“The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula One World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport.

“Following the milestone opening of the new FIA Remote Operations Centre and strengthening of officiating development through initiatives such as the FIA High Performance Programme, this development will help to build greater expertise and continuity within our stewarding structure, strengthening our ability to review and improve regulations, support the development of future officials and ensure the highest standards of consistent officiating across all our championships.”

title: Why Cadillac have stuck with Bottas for 2027
excerpt:
When Cadillac announced Bottas and Perez would form their line-up for 2026, they highlighted the fact they had 527 Grands Prix and 16 victories between them was critical the call to sign the veteran duo.

The American team knew their debut in Formula 1 would be a challenge, so they wanted to tap into that immense experience. And they've needed every bit of that knowledge this year in what has turned out to be a difficult and yet point-less debut campaign.

They've struggled with reliability all year, suffering 14 DNFs - of which Bottas has had nine - and one DNS (that was Bottas), and while the performance in certain phases has raised hopes of making it into Q2 or fighting in the lower end of the midfield, it's been fleeting rather than consistent.

That's why they moved to lock down Perez on a new multi-year deal, which was announced in Mexico and will keep him at the team until at least the end of 2029.

They were then mulling whether to activate a second year of a multi-year deal with Bottas or promote American reserve driver Colton Herta to a race seat. It made sense to give this consideration given at some point, they do want to put an American driver in the car based on merit.

On pure results, Bottas has been outperformed by Perez. The Mexican leads the qualifying head-to-head 11-9 and the race head-to-head 6-1. When it comes to fastest laps, Perez is 15-3 clear and is the only one of the two to have spent time in the top-10 during a race, albeit only one lap.

'We can get rid of the noise' – Bottas after future confirmed

However, it's not really fair to compare results given that Cadillac are trying so many different things each weekend in a bid to accelerate their progress and become midfield contenders in the first instance.

It means that both drivers have not been chasing ultimate performance but rather focusing on learning about and experimenting with the car and understanding reliability issues that tend to impact brand-new teams.

When you look at those metrics, which are hard to access externally, Cadillac have been very happy with what Bottas has delivered alongside Perez. They also know that with so many retirements, it's been difficult for Bottas to get any momentum or get a fair shot at showing his best self.

Looking at the overall project, they accept they need that expertise if they are to make some decent progress over the winter and into next season.

With that in mind, and in the knowledge that Bottas and Perez get on well and have worked together impressively this year, Cadillac opted to stick rather than twist and keep Bottas onboard for 2027 - and this gives 10-time winner Bottas another chance to show what he can do and keep his place for the future.

What does this mean for Herta?

It's a good question. Cadillac have heavily invested in Herta's development since bringing him over from the United States and backing him in a debut Formula 2 campaign alongside embedding him inside the F1 team through six FP1 appearances.

On the F2 side of things, life has been pretty hard. He's managed just four finishes in the points to sit 19th in the Drivers' Standings. On the F1 side, things have been better. The 26-year-old is believed to have impressed the team with the way he handled all six sessions and has shown strong progression.

Critically, the mileage in FP1 has earned him a Super Licence that means Cadillac now have the option to put him in the car in the next few years. Time was running out to get that licence, as a big chunk of his points were set to expire at the end of this year and achieving such a big haul would be challenging next year.

We saw firsthand with Haas how tricky it was for rookie Mick Schumacher and Nikita Mazepin in 2021 to make headway and show their talent with an underdeveloped car. By putting Herta in a Cadillac now, it would have been similarly difficult and risked burning him.

GALLERY: Cadillac reveal special livery for Las Vegas

He can now focus on continuing to prepare himself for an opportunity on the grid while giving Cadillac more time to improve their overall operation.

And that wait might not be that long. There is still a chance of him stepping up in 2028 given Cadillac only confirmed Bottas for 2027.

It'll be interesting to see what Herta and Cadillac do next, with the team yet to announce their roster of test and reserve drivers for next season - but their decision gives them plenty of options going forward.

title: The F1 Fantasy Strategist on Las Vegas and Qatar
excerpt:
Formula 1 opens the final triple header of 2026 with two night races in eight days, and each weekend asks a different question of your F1 Fantasy line-up.

The Las Vegas Strip Circuit rewards straight-line efficiency and quick tyre warm-up in cold conditions, with the heavy braking zones around the circuit offering the best overtaking opportunities of the weekend. The Lusail International Circuit then flips the test, its relentless high-speed corners punishing tyres and placing the emphasis firmly on Qualifying.

Planning your approach across both weekends together, rather than one at a time, can give players an edge. With two deadlines inside eight days, retaining enough cost-cap flexibility to react will position the best F1 Fantasy line-ups for the closing stretch of the season.

There’s also one final mini-league of the season to consider, the Williams Mini-League, which concludes in Las Vegas and is your last chance to play for signed Williams prizes and merchandise. The winner will receive an official team cap signed by Williams drivers Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon, with more details below.

It is never too late to join the free-to-play game and compete for great prizes on offer every race week. New players simply need to select five drivers and two constructors within the starting cost cap of $100 million.

If you need a reminder of all the action from Sao Paulo to help you choose your lineup, watch the highlights below. Remember to lock in your teams before Qualifying begins in Las Vegas at 2000 local time (0400 UTC on Saturday), and again in Lusail at 2100 local time (1800 UTC).

Global League update

P1 leads the Global League on 5,819 points, built on a Red Bull and Ferrari constructor pairing with Max Verstappen taking the 2x Boost.

P2 closed the gap with a well-timed No Negative chip in Brazil, clearing the weekend’s negative scores, and like the leader they ran Verstappen on the 2x Boost with Isack Hadjar and a Ferrari driver alongside.

P3 rounds out the top three, and the common thread is proactive 2x Boost and constructor management: all three backed Verstappen for the 2x Boost, a call worth 130 points, and each ran a Ferrari driver on the way to 345 points or more in Brazil, none of them carrying a Mercedes asset.

F1 Fantasy Strategist watchlist

Our F1 Fantasy Strategist evaluates seven in-game assets below and reviews potential chip strategies to help you challenge for the top step in F1 Fantasy’s global leaderboard.

Max Verstappen ($29.1m)

Max Verstappen has collected the Driver of the Day award in six of his last seven outings, worth 10 fantasy points each time, and he leads the grid with 8.3 overtakes per race across the last three weekends.

That form produced 65 fantasy points in Brazil, where he climbed from 21st to second, and he heads to Las Vegas as the winner in 2023 and 2025 before a Qatar Grand Prix he has won three years running.

Lando Norris ($26.0m)

Lando Norris secured his third win of the season in Brazil, converting pole position into victory for a 36-point fantasy return and his best score since the summer break.

He crossed the line second in Las Vegas last year before a post-race disqualification, and he has finished in the top four in two of the last three Qatar Grands Prix.

Liam Lawson ($11.7m)

Liam Lawson has four double-digit hauls in his last five race weekends, including 27 fantasy points in Mexico, and he qualified third at Interlagos last time out.

The Kiwi is the second-best value driver on the grid between Singapore and Brazil, returning 1.5 points per $1 million spent and arrives at a track that rewards consistency and reliability.

Carlos Sainz ($7.8m)

Carlos Sainz has averaged 6.7 fantasy points per race from Baku onwards, though Las Vegas has consistently brought out his best.

The Spaniard has finished in the top six on all three visits to the Las Vegas Strip Circuit, taking sixth and third for Ferrari before fifth for Williams last season.

Nico Hulkenberg ($7.2m)

Nico Hulkenberg has made 5.9 overtakes per race from Madrid onwards, the most of any driver on the grid, and started on the second row in Brazil.

The German has also finished in the points on his last two visits to Las Vegas – another good omen for a fantastic fantasy asset this season.

Other drivers to monitor: George Russell, Oscar Piastri

Mercedes ($34.0m)

Mercedes wrapped up the Drivers’ and Teams’ Championships across the last two races, and their average of 77.7 fantasy points per race is the highest of any constructor throughout the season.

They also lead all constructors for fastest pit stop, Qualifying teamwork and fastest lap points per race, which has made them the set-and-forget pick of 2026.

McLaren ($33.3m)

McLaren have scored 168 fantasy points across the two US-based races of 2026 so far, an average of 84.0 that compares with 49.3 across the season.

The Woking-based team arrive in Las Vegas having posted 63 points in Brazil, their best return since the Italian Grand Prix.

Other constructors to monitor: Red Bull, Racing Bulls

Chip strategy – Final Fix

The Final Fix allows you to replace one driver in your line-up after the team lock deadline has passed and before the Grand Prix begins, provided you have the budget to afford the replacement.

Las Vegas averages 108 overtakes across the last three seasons and should provide plenty of passing through the three straight-mode zones around the circuit, whereas Lusail is one of the harder venues on the calendar to overtake at.

Focus the chip on the potential for grid penalties in Las Vegas, where Qualifying runs a full day before the race and leaves time to react if one of your drivers is moved down the order, with three practice sessions beforehand to inform the call.

This is your last chance to join the Williams Mini-League, which concludes at the Las Vegas Grand Prix. Build your ultimate team, compete against fellow fans and put your F1 knowledge to the test for the chance to win signed Williams prizes and merchandise.

First place wins an official team cap signed by Williams drivers Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon. With the league decided in Las Vegas, a Final Fix played that weekend counts towards your mini-league score as well as the Global League.

Keep your eyes peeled for exciting mini-leagues opening later in the F1 Fantasy season, providing you with even more opportunities to play and win.

title: Facts, stats and trivia ahead of the 2026 Las Vegas GP
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season heads towards its closing stages this weekend as the Las Vegas Grand Prix kicks off the final triple header on the calendar.

Free Practice 1 and 2 will take place on Thursday, November 19, followed by Free Practice 3 and Qualifying on Friday, November 20, and the Grand Prix itself on Saturday, November 21.

Vital statistics

First Grand Prix – 2023

Track Length – 6.201km

Lap record – 1m 33.365s, Max Verstappen, Red Bull, 2025

Most pole positions – Charles Leclerc, George Russell and Lando Norris (1)

Most wins – Max Verstappen (2)

Trivia – F1 previously staged two races in Las Vegas in the early 1980s under the Caesars Palace Grand Prix moniker

Pole run to Turn 1 braking point – 160 metres

Safety Car probability – 33%*

Virtual Safety Car probability – 67%*

Pit stop time loss – 19.96 seconds (including 2.5s stop)

*From the previous three races in Las Vegas

The driver’s verdict

Jolyon Palmer, former Renault F1 driver: The track comprises long straights and slower corners. The long straights will necessitate slashing the downforce levels, so the cars will feel inherently skittish before you even factor in the cool temperatures. Building and maintaining tyre temperatures will also be tricky.

Turn 6 into 7 is one of the toughest braking zones, accelerating through a long left-hander before hitting the brakes for 7 – it’ll be easy to lock the inside front there.

Turn 12 is also crucial as it punctuates two long straights. Finding the balance between braking well and preparing the exit is tough, and mistakes here are punishing.

Having good braking ability and traction will be the key and, in general, corner exits will be crucial onto the long straights.

Everything you need to know about the Las Vegas Strip Circuit

Las Vegas GP polesitters

2025 – Lando Norris (McLaren)

2024 – George Russell (Mercedes)

2023 – Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)

Las Vegas GP winners

2025 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024 – George Russell (Mercedes)

2023 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Tyre and strategy insight

“Tyre loads are not particularly high, with the exception of the middle sector, which features several high-speed corners,” reads Pirelli’s weekend preview. “Graining could once again make an appearance due to the low grip levels and cool temperatures, as seen in previous editions of the race. In this case, degradation would be primarily mechanical in nature.

“Another factor to monitor will be brake lock-ups. The long straights end in demanding braking zones, where the risk of flat spots can become significant in both Qualifying and the race. Drivers will therefore need to avoid locking the front tyres at the most critical points of the circuit in order not to compromise a set of tyres.

“On paper, the fastest strategy is likely to be a one-stop race, with all three compounds potentially playing a role. Even the C5, which in its current specification has demonstrated good versatility, could represent a valid option for a race stint.

“The characteristics of this circuit also reduce the effectiveness of the traditional undercut strategy. Following a pit stop, tyres tend to lose temperature quickly along the long section between the pit-exit and the more demanding parts of the lap, reducing the advantage normally associated with fresh tyres.

“Last year's edition was affected by rain during Qualifying, resulting in extensive use of wet-weather tyres. Should similar conditions arise again, the full wet could prove particularly effective. The low temperatures and circuit layout favour a tyre with a deeper tread pattern, capable of generating and retaining temperature more easily than the intermediate.”

Current form

One week on from Kimi Antonelli securing his maiden World Championship, Mercedes sealed the 2026 constructors’ title last time out in Sao Paulo – but with a final triple header still to play out, the Silver Arrows will be keen to end their triumphant season on a positive note.

The team know what it is like to win in Las Vegas, having tasted victory with George Russell back in 2024. However, it is Max Verstappen who has the strongest record from the race’s short history after standing on the top step of the podium in 2023 and 2025.

Red Bull will be keen to add another success to that list as they look to keep McLaren at bay in the battle for P3 of the Teams’ Championship, off the back of Lando Norris’ third win of the season at Interlagos.

Ferrari, meanwhile, look safe in second place but will be hoping for a better outing in Las Vegas, with Team Principal Fred Vasseur admitting after the Sao Paulo Grand Prix that the Scuderia had been lacking performance during the weekend.

Elsewhere, Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad arrive into the event with their futures sealed – both having recently been confirmed as staying with the team in 2027 – while Haas’ new recruit Rafael Camara is set for his second F1 weekend following his debut in Brazil.

At the lower end of the standings, Cadillac remain the only squad without a point to their name as they prepare for another home event. Can the American outfit get off the mark during the final triple header?

Iconic moment

It has only been on the calendar for a few years, but the Las Vegas Grand Prix immediately provided plenty of action and drama in the inaugural 2023 race – none more so than when Charles Leclerc made a stunning last-lap pass on Sergio Perez.

title: Everything you need to know about the Las Vegas Strip Circuit
excerpt:
Formula 1 returns to action with the Las Vegas Grand Prix this weekend. But how much do you know about the Las Vegas Strip Circuit? F1.com presents your all-in-one guide…

Key Las Vegas statistics

Circuit length: 6.201km

Number of turns: 17

Number of laps: 50

Race distance: 309.958km

Lap record: 1m 33.365s – Max Verstappen (2025)

When was the Las Vegas Strip Circuit’s first Grand Prix?

Las Vegas previously staged two F1 races in the early 1980s under the name of the Caesars Palace Grand Prix – but when the City of Lights returned to the calendar in 2023, it saw the debut of the brand-new Las Vegas Strip Circuit.

Located in the heart of the city, the 17-turn street circuit sweeps past iconic sights such as the Caesars Palace, the Bellagio and the Venetian.

Three years on from launching with a memorable maiden Grand Prix in 2023, the Las Vegas Strip Circuit will host its fourth Formula 1 event this year.

What’s the circuit like to drive?

With average speeds similar to Monza – the famed Italian track known as the ‘Temple of Speed’ – the Las Vegas Strip Circuit provides plenty of opportunities for action and overtaking.

Jolyon Palmer, former Renault F1 driver, says: “The track comprises long straights and slower corners.

“The long straights will necessitate slashing the downforce levels, so the cars will feel inherently skittish before you even factor in the cool temperatures. Building and maintaining tyre temperatures will also be tricky.

“Turn 6 into 7 is one of the toughest braking zones, accelerating through a long left-hander before hitting the brakes for 7 – it’ll be easy to lock the inside front there.

“Turn 12 is also crucial as it punctuates two long straights. Finding the balance between braking well and preparing the exit is tough, and mistakes here are punishing.

“Having good braking ability and traction will be the key and, in general, corner exits will be crucial onto the long straights.”

The long straights will necessitate slashing the downforce levels, so the cars will feel inherently skittish before you even factor in the cool temperatures. Building and maintaining tyre temperatures will also be tricky.Jolyon Palmer

Where are the Straight Mode zones and overtake detection?

As a reminder, and as explained in our pre-season summary of regulation changes, Straight Mode is a different aerodynamic configuration that allows cars to reduce their drag, making them more efficient when accelerating up towards top speed.

The rear wing continues to open up a gap – just like it did when drivers used DRS (the Drag Reduction System) in the past – but now the front wing also moves. The uppermost front wing elements drop down at the same time the rear wing’s top element does.

This is a mode that is used on every single lap in dry conditions, in every area that is designated for it. Essentially, the car will adapt between two different configurations depending on where it is on the track, providing maximum downforce in corners but then less drag on straights.

At the Las Vegas Strip Circuit, there are three designated Straight Mode zones: the first is situated on the run between Turns 4 and 5, followed by the long section between Turns 12 and 14, and a final zone between Turns 16 and 17.

Meanwhile, Overtake Mode replaces DRS and is a new power mode that allows a driver to recharge more electrical energy, and generate an additional electrical power profile, so they can sustain a higher speed for a longer period.

There is one detection point per lap for this mode – expected to be out of the final corner on many occasions, leading onto a long straight – and it will be available to drivers on the following lap as long as they stay within a second of the car in front at that detection point.

The Overtake Detection marker here comes just out of Turn 16, while the Overtake Activation line follows on the straight towards Turn 17.

Five fun facts about the Las Vegas Grand Prix

The Las Vegas Grand Prix is held on a Saturday, marking a change from the usual weekend format

Max Verstappen has the best record so far at the event, having won the inaugural race in 2023 before scoring another victory in 2025 as well as setting a new lap record

The race is the only one on the calendar where McLaren have raced more than three times and never finished in the top five, with both cars disqualified in 2025 due to technical infringements

A different driver has claimed pole position at every Las Vegas Grand Prix to date – Charles Leclerc was the first to do so in 2023, followed by George Russell and Lando Norris

Las Vegas became the third race on the calendar to be held in the United States when it arrived in 2023, joining Miami and Austin

title: Camara offers update on plans for final races of 2026
excerpt:
Rafael Camara is preparing for his second Formula 1 appearance with Haas at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, but a decision is yet to be reached on whether he will contest the final two rounds of the season.

Camara believes he will be better prepared for his second F1 outing after an intense debut in Sao Paulo, while admitting his plans for the final two rounds of the season remain undecided.

The 21-year-old Brazilian made his F1 debut at Interlagos following Esteban Ocon's departure from Haas, navigating challenging weather conditions before finishing 20th in his first Grand Prix.

Having been confirmed for another appearance alongside team mate Ollie Bearman in Las Vegas, Camara is hoping to build on the lessons learned in Brazil as he tackles another unfamiliar circuit.

"It was a very intense weekend, but there was a lot to learn, and it will be very useful this weekend," he said. "I'm excited to race here. Obviously, it will be my first time in Vegas, so I'm trying to prepare in the best way."

Unlike his last-minute call-up in Brazil, Camara has had more time to familiarise himself with the demands of a Grand Prix weekend, leaving him feeling more at ease ahead of his second outing.

"Mentally, it will be easier because I've had more time to prepare and everything feels a bit more normal," he explained. "Having already experienced some things in Brazil, I'm calmer and know a bit more about what to expect. I think it's just maybe thinking less and doing the driving more."

While Camara is confirmed to race for Haas in 2027, he admitted a decision is yet to be made on whether he will contest the final two Grands Prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi or return to Formula 2.

"That is a good question, even to myself," he admitted. "It will be tricky to decide, but there's still a lot to happen. I'm just focused on finishing this weekend in a good way, and then we'll see what happens for the next two races."

The Brazilian added that discussions with his team would follow the Las Vegas weekend, with both options appealing to him.

"Both would be very important to me, but I still need to discuss with my team what we'll do for the next races," he said. "I would be happy with either."

Camara also spoke positively about his relationship with Haas Team Principal Ayao Komatsu, revealing that the pair had discussed his debut and the areas where he could improve.

"Overall, on this first weekend, he didn't complain about anything, so that was good," he said. "On Sunday, there were some things I would have expected to do better. But overall, it was a good weekend and very positive."

title: Piastri opens up on decision to split with management team
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has explained why he and his management team, led by Mark and Ann Webber, mutually agreed to part ways, with the Australian believing the time was right for a new chapter in his career.

The decision was announced following the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, bringing an end to a partnership that began in 2019 and helped Piastri secure his Formula 1 debut with McLaren in 2023.

Speaking to the media in Las Vegas, Piastri reflected on the contribution the Webbers had made to his career, explaining that both parties had reached a point where pursuing separate paths felt like the right decision.

"We were just getting to a stage in our collaboration where it was better for us to go on our separate paths," he said.

"Mark and Ann contributed so much to my career, both in placing me where I am today and the management of everything behind the scenes that nobody ever really sees. It felt like the time was right for something new."

The Webbers had already reduced their trackside involvement during the 2026 season, with Piastri's former PREMA race engineer Pedro Matos and mental coach Emma Murray taking on greater roles within his close team.

Asked whether a different management structure could benefit his performances, Piastri reiterated his appreciation for the support he had received throughout his junior career and first four seasons in F1.

"Mark played a massive part in my career, both Mark and Ann, at the end of my junior career, setting me up in Formula 1 and guiding me through those first few years," he added. "The impact they've had on my career has been enormous, and I think now it feels like the right time for us both to go on our separate adventures.

"I think having the structure around you is an important thing, and it has looked a bit different this year already and will look a bit different again in the future, probably. But they played a big part in where my career is today, so I'm very, very grateful for everything they did."

While Piastri looks ahead to a new chapter off the track, his immediate focus remains on maximising his results in the final three rounds of the 2026 season, beginning with a challenging weekend in Las Vegas.

The McLaren driver will serve a 10-place grid penalty after taking a new internal combustion engine, although the team are also introducing further aerodynamic upgrades, including a new floor

"Vegas is always unique as a weekend, and as an event," the Australian driver explained when asked about how he plans to approach the race.

"We're going to be starting a little further behind, no matter where we qualify, so it's just trying to maximise what we can. We don't know exactly where we're going to sit with things. Hopefully, the new engine is going to help out a little bit, but there's obviously going to be some spots to make up."

Despite some frustrating results in recent rounds, Piastri believes his feeling with the MCL40 has improved, particularly in Malaysia, Singapore, Baku and Brazil. The Australian pointed to his race pace at Interlagos as an encouraging sign, even if his qualifying performance prevented him from fully capitalising on that potential.

"I felt like through Malaysia, Singapore and Baku, and then Brazil as well, the results weren't always what they could have been, but the feeling in the car was definitely an improvement," he explained. "In Brazil, Qualifying was a shame because the pace I had on Sunday was the strongest that it's been for a while.

"That's the big positive. It's just about trying to convert that potential now into results."

title: 'I want to fight for the victory' in Las Vegas – Russell
excerpt:
George Russell has stated he wants "to fight for the victory and I think we can do it" in this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, having decided against taking a new turbo for his Mercedes.

The German manufacturer enters this weekend having clinched the Constructors' Championship last time out in Brazil, while Kimi Antonelli became the youngest drivers' champion at the previous round in Mexico.

Even with the pressure somewhat off the team for the remaining three rounds, a new turbo is set to be introduced with all eyes firmly fixed on finding greater performance for 2027.

Speaking on Wednesday's media day in Las Vegas, Russell stated he would not be taking the new part to avoid any grid penalty, having been given the choice himself by the team.

"I think with the performance benefit it brings, it's not huge. It's just a step in the direction as a team we want to take," he said.

"We're lucky with Mercedes that there's eight drivers running the power unit. I think five or six of them are taking the turbo, the two or three who aren't, including myself, is just because it would mean a back of grid penalty and Vegas is a track I've gone well at in the past, I enjoy it here.

"The decision I was very much involved in, they said 'if you want to take it, you can take it, if you don't, you don't'. I was happy not to because I want to fight for the victory and I think we can do it, with or without it."

Russell claimed victory in Las Vegas in 2024 and finished second last year, with the Briton hopeful of another strong result this season.

Russell currently sits third in the drivers' standings, 17 points behind Max Verstappen, but admits that finding performance over the remaining races is his main priority.

"For me what's more important is just to have some strong weekends," said Russell when asked about trying to reach P2 in the standings.

"And that doesn't necessarily just mean the result, it just means from FP1 through the weekend, showing good performances. This season it's been so up and down, even during my strong weekends, other than Baku, sometimes it hasn't been every lap of the weekend.

"That's the most important to me. Of course I'd love to finish as high as possible but that's the most important."

Team mate Antonelli stated that "we don't expect any major performance gain from" the new turbo, but that it will help more with reliability and driveability.

The new World Champion also admitted that he will try and aid Russell in his bid to finish P2 in the championship.

"On my side, first of all, I'll try to do my best and try to win as much as possible," said the Italian.

"But if there is an occasion where I need to eventually help, I'll do it for sure. I'll be a team player.

"But the main focus now is to try to win as much as possible, try to win the remaining races and finish on a high, and carry the momentum into 2027."

title: Breaking: FIA to introduce full-time stewards for F1 from 2027
excerpt:
This is a major step change for the FIA and Formula 1

The FIA has confirmed it will appoint full-time stewards to Formula 1 for the first time, beginning a phased rollout from the 2027 season.

The governing body says the move is designed to bring greater consistency and dedication to race officiating at the highest level of the sport.

A small number of full-time stewards will be recruited during the 2027 campaign, with the FIA aiming to expand that group further for the 2028 season and beyond.

Existing FIA stewards will not be replaced. They will continue working alongside the new recruits as part of a mixed roster of full-time and part-time officials for the foreseeable future.

Driver stewards will keep their role at each event, with the federation recognising the specialist knowledge they bring.

The FIA has now launched a recruitment drive for experienced international stewards to form the first generation of full-time officials, who will work alongside its existing pool of qualified stewards.

Building towards a bigger department

The federation says the dedicated full-time structure will provide continuity and expertise, supporting its ongoing review of sporting regulations and stewarding guidelines.

It is also expected to allow for deeper implementation of best practice and greater consistency in decision-making across race weekends.

Beyond the grands prix themselves, the FIA says the new stewards will have increased capacity to spot emerging trends and flag areas requiring regulatory clarification, feeding into the evolution of the sporting regulations.

They will also be tasked with training and mentoring future generations of FIA officials, contributing to the FIA High Performance Programme and pushing for greater harmonisation across the federation's championships.

[Article continues below]

The plan is for the department to grow in the coming years to between 12 and 15 full-time stewards, a structure that would eventually extend support to other FIA single-seater championships.

The move is the latest step in a restructuring of officiating at the top of motorsport that began under FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem at the start of his mandate, following a reorganisation of Race Control in 2022, the creation of the FIA Officials department, and sustained investment in FIA Systems Operations.

Last month, the FIA opened an all-new Remote Operations Centre at Biggin Hill in the UK, a facility built to maintain the highest standards of race management.

The federation says the financial turnaround under Ben Sulayem's leadership has made the stewarding programme possible, allowing it to reinvest in its core sporting responsibilities.

Ben Sulayem said the appointment of full-time stewards reflects the FIA's commitment to decision-making standards in the sport.

"This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport," said Ben Sulayem.

"The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula One World Championship; it is also an investment in the future of our sport."

"Following the milestone opening of the new FIA Remote Operations Centre and strengthening of officiating development through initiatives such as the FIA High Performance Programme, this development will help to build greater expertise and continuity within our stewarding structure, strengthening our ability to review and improve regulations, support the development of future officials and ensure the highest standards of consistent officiating across all our championships."

title: Sergio Perez welcomes Cadillac 'distraction' end as 2027 lineup confirmed
excerpt:
Sergio Perez has welcomed the end of a lingering distraction after Cadillac confirmed its 2027 driver lineup, with Valtteri Bottas set to remain his teammate following weeks of speculation that linked the Finn's seat to Colton Herta.

Cadillac confirmed on Wednesday that it had exercised its contract option to keep Bottas for a second season, ending uncertainty that had built up after Perez himself was signed to an extension earlier in the year while Bottas's deal contained only a team option rather than a guaranteed drive.

Herta had picked up the FIA superlicence points required to race in Formula 1 through practice outings in Austin, Mexico City and Sao Paulo, fuelling talk that the American, backed by TWG Motorsports, could be fast-tracked into the second Cadillac seat for the team's second year on the grid.

Cadillac instead opted for continuity, pointing to Bottas's experience as crucial to resolving the reliability problems, including recurring brake cooling and suspension issues, that hampered the American outfit's debut campaign.

Asked how happy he is to continue with Bottas, Perez told select media, including RacingNews365: "Ah, very. I think I work well with Valtteri. I think he brings a lot of speed, a lot of experience to the team, and I think at this stage it's crucial.

"I've always said, I think the team has much more important things to focus on than drivers for now. So, yeah, happy in that regard. Now we can take that distraction out of our way and make sure that operationally we can make good stops, can do good things, because the last few races operationally have been weak."

Sergio Perez 'happy' for Valtteri Bottas partnership continuation

Perez also revealed he had been mindful of the pressure the rumours placed on his teammate throughout the process.

Discussing whether he had asked Bottas how he felt during the contract speculation, Perez said:

"I mean, obviously, I was aware of the situation, and it's not easy as a teammate to know what's fully going on, and all you can do is just support and, yeah, hope for the best for your teammate. You know that you are spending a lot of time with him, and I'm happy, really, he's staying."

title: Oscar Piastri confirms 'interim' arrangement after surprise Mark Webber exit
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has had his say over the surprise split with Mark and Ann Webber from his management team.

Oscar Piastri has confirmed that he is currently working with an "interim" management set-up after the surprise exits of Mark and Ann Webber.

It was announced on the Monday following the Sao Paulo Grand Prix that Piastri would split with the Webbers with immediate effect, with the Webbers having guided Piastri up from the junior categories to F1, where he made his debut in 2023.

Despite the odd timing of the announcement, Piastri has explained that there is not a ready-to-go replacement for the Webbers, and that for the time being, he is working with an "interim" management set-up.

"I don't have anyone confirmed," Piastri replied when asked by RacingNews365 if he was going to take his time to assess the options around him.

"I've obviously got an interim set-up at the moment, but nothing is set in stone for the future.

"I'll define that in due course."

[Article continues below]

Piastri on Webber exit

Turning to the Webbers, Piastri spoke of the "massive role" they had played in bringing him into F1 after a stellar junior career, including back-to-back titles in FIA F2 and FIA F3.

"They played a massive role in my career and getting to this point - the end of my junior career and the start of my F1 career.

"The support at the track and behind the scenes was incredibly valuable, and I think now is the appropriate time to go our separate ways and do new things.

"I haven't got anything set in stone at the moment. I am still looking at what the future looks like, for the team around me."

title: Liam Lawson admits to 'strange' feeling despite landing new F1 contract
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has explained the "strange" feeling he holds despite landing a 2027 Racing Bulls F1 contract before the end of the season.

Weeks of speculation ended last week when it was formally announced that Lawson, who is a strong ninth in the championship with 89 points and the highest-placed non-Mercedes, Ferrari, Red Bull, or McLaren driver, would be kept on for 2027.

There had been serious doubt about his seat with Red Bull evaluating F2 protege Nikola Tsolov for potential promotion, but the Bulgarian must make do with a third and reserve driver role at both Red Bull and Racing Bulls in 2027.

For New Zealander Lawson, knowing his future before the end of the season is something he is unaccustomed to, as he explained.

"It's obviously a good feeling, a little bit of relief for me. It's a little bit strange, just because I've actually not really done races or finished the season knowing a little bit early," Lawson told media, including RacingNews365.

"I feel like it is more normal to do that, but for us at least, it hasn't been in the past, so it's a little bit of a strange feeling, but it's obviously nice.

"And for me, I'll try and enjoy the last few races even more. I mean, I honestly have enjoyed racing a lot this year, especially the second half, despite everything going on in the background.

"I'm just going to try and keep that rolling through the last couple of races."

[Article continues below]

Lawson doubt

When then asked if there was a moment he feared he would not get the nod for 2027, Lawson conceded to having doubts at times.

"I don't think so, not really. I mean, if I look back to last year, I feel like I was thinking about it a lot, and it was definitely... You have a lot of doubts always, especially when things aren't going well," he said.

"But I feel like for us this year, things have been just quite strong across the board. Especially since the summer break; things have been really, really good for us as a team. We've had a strong car across all the tracks, and I feel like we've executed mostly each weekend.

"So I didn't feel like I struggled to find a reason why, but obviously you think about it, and it's talked about a lot. But I feel like, more than anything, I just tried to remove that sort of thought process from my mind as much as I could and just try to focus and enjoy driving the car.

"And I felt like we were able to do that."

title: Kimi Antonelli explains reason to fear Red Bull in Las Vegas 'outlier'
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli expects Red Bull to be Mercedes' main rival at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, where the long straights play to the strengths of its combustion engine and low-drag 'Macarena' rear wing.

The teams' two power units have different strengths. Red Bull has held the advantage on internal combustion engine performance in the FIA's ADUO assessments this season, a significant achievement in what is its first campaign as a power unit manufacturer.

But Antonelli also highlighted how Mercedes has the edge in how efficiently it managed energy from the battery, a particular challenge over the lap in Las Vegas, which is a power-sensitive circuit.

Nonetheless, the F1 drivers' champion expects the RB22 to be a formidable challenge in Sin City.

"Red Bull is going to be very strong this weekend," Antonelli told media, including RacingNews365.

"However, I think we're the only one who has a set of wings that have slightly lower downforce, so a bit less draggy. So it's gonna be interesting. Let's see if we're gonna use it here.

"But definitely, it's gonna be very interesting. Our power unit has been very strong on the electrical side.

"Obviously, also on the combustion side, but the electrical side has been very strong. I think we're probably the most efficient ones in terms of electrical power and efficiency.

"However, Red Bull as well; they have a very strong power unit, and their car is very efficient on the straight, especially with the Macarena wing they have. So, I think it's gonna be very interesting."

[Article continues below]

Why Las Vegas is an 'outlier'

The cold will make it difficult for drivers to get their tyres up to temperature, and Antonelli expects the grip on the street circuit to change considerably between the first two practice sessions.

It will be a critical factor once qualifying and the 50-lap race come around, with temperatures expected to start around 12 degrees Celsius for both sessions before cooling further.

"It's gonna be one of those races that is a bit of an outlier because, again, it's very difficult on energy," Antonelli added. "But it's going to be so cold, so having the tyres at the right temperature is going to be key. So let's see.

"And also, track evolution is gonna be massive. I think FP1 is gonna be drifting, and then maybe FP2 is gonna be back to normal driving.

"I think our main competitor will be Red Bull this weekend, probably McLaren as well. Let's see also Ferrari, how they're going to do."

title: Isack Hadjar makes defiant Red Bull statement despite being 'happy' for Liam Lawson
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar insists he does not feel "threatened" by Liam Lawson or any of the other drivers in the Red Bull programme, claiming he does not look at the "queue" behind him.

In partnering Max Verstappen at the top team, Hadjar holds the most coveted seat for those at Racing Bulls or in the academy, but is not concerned about who might be vying for his job.

The French driver appears to have locked down the second drive at Red Bull for the foreseeable future. Not only will he continue alongside the four-time F1 drivers' champion next season, but he has achieved the rare feat of keeping his position clear of rumour and speculation, something many of the Dutchman's team-mates have been unable to do.

Even having missed three rounds through injury, Hadjar has done enough to impress the top brass at the energy drinks-backed team, taking three podiums, in Monaco, Baku and São Paulo.

Lawson, who deputised in his RB22 whilst Hadjar was sidelined, has also earned considerable praise. Recently confirmed to have kept his seat with Racing Bulls for 2027, the delay in securing the New Zealander's services was widely questioned across the paddock.

Asked whether he had congratulated his former team-mate yet, Hadjar was quick to voice his support for the 24-year-old.

"No, but I'm happy for him, though, because he's had a very strong season," he told media, including RacingNews365.

"I was his team-mate last year, and I got a taste of how good [and] complete he was as a driver, so I was not very surprised in the end.

"You give him a car that can score every weekend, and he does it. So, yeah, fair play."

[Article continues below]

Hadjar: 'I don't really feel threatened by anything'

However, despite Lawson's standout form, which has seen him single-handedly outscore Alpine in the fight for fifth in the constructors' championship, Hadjar is adamant he does not need to worry.

The 22-year-old does not appear to be feeling the pressure from Lawson, Arvid Lindblad or Nikola Tsolov, who is fighting for this year's F2 championship and will step up to the team's reserve role next term.

"My whole career, I've never looked backwards, so I'm focusing on... And I achieved my goal to be at Red Bull," Hadjar said.

"I'm here to stay for a while, so I don't really feel threatened by anything. I proved my point last year in my rookie season at Racing Bulls.

"I'm doing my job pretty well here at Red Bull for my first year. Next year is going to be better, so I don't really look at the queue behind me."

title: Haas respond to Oliver Bearman contract frustrations with unwavering stance
excerpt:
Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu has described Oliver Bearman’s frustration at the wait for a new contract as "understandable" and insisted the British driver will race for the team in next season.

Speaking on media day at the Las Vegas Grand Prix just hours before Komatsu’s remarks, Bearman said even members of his own team had been asking why Haas had yet to announce him.

The 21-year-old expects to partner Rafael Camara in 2027, but his is the final seat on the grid awaiting confirmation.

"It's just a difficult situation, and I don't think there's any excuse to be standing here at this stage without anything to tell you," Bearman said.

Asked how he keeps the Ferrari junior motivated while the talks continue, Komatsu pointed to what he sees from his driver each weekend, whilst insisting there is no way the Briton does not partner Camara next year.

"I don't think he needs motivation. He's very, very motivated," the Haas boss told media, including RacingNews365. "I think you can see that week in, week out. That's not an issue at all.

"But the contract, it just takes some time to align everyone, finalise everything. But there's no... everybody's aligned.

"Ollie wants to drive for us; we want order in the car, so there's no doubt it's gonna happen. It's a bit unfortunate it's taking a long time, but it's gonna happen."

Komatsu had already dismissed suggestions at the Mexico City Grand Prix that Bearman's salary demands were holding up a deal.

It is understood that talks between Bearman's management and Ferrari have centred on his options beyond 2027 if Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton stay on and there is no seat for him at Maranello.

Komatsu was pressed on whether the tension lay with the Italian team and whether Haas could retain Bearman without the Scuderia's backing.

"There are many parties involved in, let's say, contractual restoration," he said. "I don't want to go into detail, but there's no doubt he's going to be in the car next year. It will happen."

title: Lewis Hamilton addresses Ferrari communication after ignoring instructions
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton is adamant there is not a "trust" issue with his Ferrari race engineer after twice ignoring calls to pit in recent races.

Hamilton explained he "didn't have the information" he required on the two occasions, in Singapore and Brazil, when Carlo Santi instructed him to come in, but dismissed the suggestion that there is a greater problem with how the pair communicate over team radio.

Last year, his first with Ferrari, the British driver struggled to gel with Riccardo Adami, with the change in personnel made ahead of the current campaign.

This has seen a significant step forward in how the partnership between driver and pit wall works, even if Hamilton has taken the strategy into his own hands a couple of times more recently.

Asked about the pair of incidents, both of which ultimately cost the 41-year-old positions, Hamilton told media, including RacingNews365: "No, it's definitely not a trust thing.

"We're constantly working on our communication. I think that it's been a lot better this year.

"Carlo has done an amazing job, and I think there's been a couple of times where... it's just those particular two times — particularly the last time — was just I didn't have the information I needed, and I got the call at the last minute."

[Article continues below]

Working in the 'right direction'

Whilst this season has been an improvement, there have been a few cases of Hamilton being frustrated by the Ferrari pit wall.

Despite failing to capitalise on strategic opportunities at times, the seven-time F1 drivers' champion feels there are steady signs of improvement.

"And we'll just continue to work on the processes," the 106-time grand prix winner added.

"We're super united and working, I think, in the right direction."

title: The rarely-considered reason Las Vegas GP will be 'doubly hard' this year
excerpt:
The Las Vegas Grand Prix will present a tyre temperature challenge unlike anything drivers faced with the previous generation of cars, with George Russell pointing to the new-for-2026 Straightline Mode (SM) as a significant complicating factor.

Unlike the old DRS system, which only adjusted the rear wing flap and was not always available to drivers every lap during races, SM mode opens moveable flaps on both the front and rear wings simultaneously. It is available to all cars on designated straights, stripping away far more downforce than DRS ever did.

That matters enormously in Las Vegas, where night-time temperatures in the Mojave Desert regularly dip into single digits in November, already making it one of the coldest rounds on the calendar.

Temperatures for the start of both qualifying and the 50-lap race this year are expected to be around 12 degrees Celsius, but will drop during the on-track action.

With less load pressing the tyres into the tarmac on the circuit's long straights, keeping rubber in its working temperature window becomes significantly harder, something that will be compounded by the rigorous energy management requirements of the power-sensitive circuit.

Russell, speaking to media including RacingNews365, explained the scale of the problem.

"It's going to be a lot harder, and one of the extra challenges this time around in Vegas is having the SM modes," the Mercedes driver said.

"So when you go down all the straights and the wings are open, there's much less downforce going through the tyres."

Russell detailed just how much load is lost once SM mode opens the wings on the back straight.

"So it's doubly hard to keep the temperature in the tyres," the eight-time grand prix winner added.

"When you're going down that back straight, 25 seconds, with hundreds of kilos less downforce than we had on the cars last year, probably even thousands of kilos less with the SM open compared to when DRS is closed, it's going to be a challenge."

title: Formula E drivers considering fresh FIA letter over 'impossible' problem
excerpt:
The Formula E drivers are considering taking action again against the FIA for the second time this year.

19 November 3:10PM

Formula E drivers are weighing up further action against the FIA after warning that the series' driver weight limit has become "impossible" for some competitors to meet, with Dan Ticktum and Oliver Rowland both raising concerns about the current regulations.

Formula E enforces a reference minimum weight of 82kg for the driver, including racewear and the seat shell, after the figure was raised from 80kg ahead of Season 11 to bring it in line with Formula 1.

But while the number on paper matches F1's own 82kg driver minimum, the seat weight behind it does not, with Formula E's standardised shells and thicker foam inserts weighing considerably more than their F1 equivalents.

Ticktum, discussing having to lose weight before the Mexico City round, told RacingNews365 that the issue has become a serious talking point in the paddock.

"Well, most of the drivers are over," said Ticktum. "Like, the minimum weight is a bit of a talking point, which I'm sure will come to light in the media at some point. Us drivers are trying to do something about it.

"It essentially depends on your car, but most cars weigh similar. You're going to have to be, like, low 70s kilos for guys that are six foot, sort of my height and above. That's quite impossible, really. Or very unhealthy."

The situation is being compounded by the arrival of the Gen4 car, which brings a significantly heavier package built around a larger 55kWh battery and permanent all-wheel-drive dual powertrains. With more weight added elsewhere on the car, drivers face even tighter margins to hit the overall minimum, intensifying pressure on taller and heavier competitors.

Asked whether another letter to the FIA, following the one sent by the drivers in March over stewarding standards, could be repeated on the weight issue, Ticktum suggested it remains a live option.

"Possibly," the Fortescue driver said. "I don't know how much I'm allowed to say at the moment. It's an avenue we might look at, more on the grounds of safety than anything."

Rowland highlights seat weight gap with F1

Rowland, who alongside Lucas di Grassi helped spearhead March's letter to FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem over race direction and stewarding, confirmed that talks over the weight limit have so far produced little progress.

"There's been talks with little resolution, so probably there'll be something," Rowland told RacingNews365. "And look, I mean, the problem, I think, at the moment is that they're kind of asking the teams, and genetically, some drivers just cannot make a weight limit.

"It's the same as Formula 1, but our seat weighs three and a half kilos more. So we're not asking for an exception to what they have in Formula 1; we're just asking for it to be equal. For example, there's some drivers here that just cannot make the weight limit the way it is at the moment, and it's unfair.

"And the whole reason the 82kg was brought in in the first place was to make that equal across drivers. And at the moment, I think we had some data and statistics that, like, nine or 10 drivers were over the limit last year, but with the car this year being more close to the limit, that's just a loss of performance.

"And I don't think it's fair that someone, just because of the way they're built, should be lacking in performance for 2027. So we'll see. Hopefully they can take it on board. I think they understand. But yeah, it's just up to them to make the right decision for our health as well. Starving yourself and dehydrating yourself before a race is not going to work."

Asked when a letter or further action might materialise, Rowland pointed to the specific weight gap drivers want closed.

"I don't know, to be honest," added Rowland. "You'd have to ask them [the FIA]. I think, as I said, in Formula 1 you're probably looking around two kilos for a seat, whereas here it's around five and a half to six kilos.

"So, I mean, the delta is three and a half to four kilos. So, I think that we're not asking for more than that at the moment. Even still, with that, it's on the limit for some of us. So, I think just to make it in line with Formula 1, I think is as fair as it can be."

RacingNews365 has approached the FIA for comment.

title: Lance Stroll responds to looming slice of unwanted F1 history
excerpt:
Lance Stroll is on the verge of attaining an unfortunate F1 record with Aston Martin, sitting just one retirement shy of equalling the most suffered in a single season.

Stroll has failed to finish 13 grands prix of the current campaign so far, with three events still to go out of the 23-round calendar for 2026.

If the Canadian is not classified in Las Vegas, Qatar or Abu Dhabi, he will match Andrea De Cesaris' slate from the 1986 and 1987 seasons, when the Italian retired 14 times for Minardi and then Brabham, respectively.

Remarkably, out of the two times he did reach the chequered flag in the latter campaign, one was a podium finish, at the third round of the year in Belgium.

Rubens Barrichello also hit the same mark in 1997, for Stewart, in the eponymous team's debut F1 season. Impressively, like De Cesaris a decade earlier, one of the Brazilian's three classified results — for the outfit that is now Red Bull — was a podium.

So all hope is not lost for Stroll, who will want to avoid failing to finish twice from the season-ending triple-header to escape taking the record outright.

The three-time podium finisher is yet to score this term and has only taken the chequered flag twice since the F1 summer break, conceding that there have been "way too many retirements" this year on his side of the Aston Martin garage.

However, despite the torrid campaign for the Silverstone-based squad and new power unit partner Honda, the 28-year-old was keen to be optimistic about the future.

When the looming stat was put to him on media day in Las Vegas, Stroll told media, including RacingNews365: "I heard about it, but... we had a lot of issues out there, a lot of engine problems.

"It's been a tough year for the whole team. We're just not nearly as competitive as we want to be, and it's been a long year for everyone.

"But all we can do is just stay positive and look forward to the future, and hopefully we'll be in a much more competitive spot next year."

title: Max Verstappen issues F1 refusal over 'invasion of privacy' concern
excerpt:
Max Verstappen says he will refuse to take part in F1's new contract with biometric tracking data company Whoop.

A new deal was announced ahead of the Las Vegas GP, where Whoop would be able to use driver biometric data in the world feed broadcast, including heart-rate data.

This would be used to chart how a driver is reacting at key stages during a grand prix or overtaking battles, with drivers required to give their permission for their own data to be used.

However, four-time drivers' champion Verstappen has declared that he will not be a part of the deal and share his private data.

"I won't be involved," Verstappen told media, including RacingNews365.

"I don't use any device for my training; I don't use anything because, first of all, I don't like to be tracked, and I know when I am tired.

"If people want to, if drivers want it, then sure, but for me, it is not something that I like and also not what I want people to see."

When it was then put to Verstappen that it would be an invasion of his privacy, the Dutchman agreed.

"Yeah," he began.

"People don't need to know my heart rate. I also don't want to know my heart rate.

"I know when it is high, and I know when it is low.

"For me, it is definitely a privacy thing, but at the same time, as I said, I don't use it privately, even for training."

title: Fernando Alonso makes F1 retirement decision ahead of looming V8 engine return
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has declared that he will not be racing in F1 when V8 engines make their return, possibly in 2030.

Talks were held earlier this week between the FIA, F1, teams, and power unit manufacturers over dropping the turbo hybrids in use since 2014 in favour of some kind of V8 machine.

The official announcement was posted by the FIA, signalling that from 2030, a 2.1L turbocharged V8 was coming, but this was quickly pulled for mysterious reasons.

Alonso, who was weighing up retirement at the end of 2026 before deciding ultimately to stay on for his 24th F1 season in 2027, has now declared that he will not be on the grid in 2030, when FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem would like to see V8s return.

Alonso has been one of the fiercest critics of the 2026 engine regulations, decrying the effect the 50:50 power output split between the ICE and batteries has had on the cars, and leading him to brand fast corners as "charging stations" for the car.

"I will not be around for the new V8, 100%," Alonso told media, including RacingNews365.

"[I have] surprised myself [in the past], but not this time. When I stop, it will be the moment to try different things.

"It is a long way ahead, but I think it will be enough.

"It is frustrating that we did not have V8s in 2014 already.

"From 2014 to 2030 or 2031, it is 16 or 17 years of pure racing lost."

Should Alonso race in F1 2030, he would turn 49 years old during the season, and would become the first F1 driver to race at that age in a world championship grand prix since Pierro Taruffi at the 1956 Italian GP.

title: Oliver Bearman voices disappointment at 'strange' Haas F1 contract delay
excerpt:
Oliver Bearman has voiced considerable "disappointment" at the delay in agreeing a new contract to stay at Haas in 2027.

Fresh terms for Bearman to continue into a third season with the team in 2027 were expected to be a formality, with the 21-year-old expected to formally become the team leader after Esteban Ocon's exit and Rafael Camara's promotion.

Warm words were given by team boss Ayao Komatsu, indicating it would just be a matter of time before the announcement was made public, but now, with just three rounds to go in the 2026 season, Bearman still has not signed.

The seat is now the only one vacant on the 2027 grid, with the news of Valtteri Bottas being kept on at Cadillac, with Bearman expressing his major distaste for the situation.

"There is nothing new, if I am honest, and I am quite disappointed that I am sitting here at round 21 without a contract signed for next year," Bearman told media, including RacingNews365.

"It is a strange situation, but we're getting there, and all I can say is that it is a bit disappointing and obviously not ideal for a driver's confidence and things like that.

"I know that I've done a good job this year, but the fact that I don't know what I am doing next year is not ideal; I can tell you that much."

Then, when asked who he was disappointed with, Bearman simply replied: "I am not going to comment on that."

The Briton then went further in his explanation of why he was feeling disappointed.

"I am certain of what I want, and it is very clear that I'm trying to stay at Haas and that I deserve to stay at Haas, at least I feel this way," he said.

"But it is a strange situation, and I really thought we had made decent progress in the last triple-header, and maybe it doesn't seem that way, so it is a little disappointing.

"But I hope we can get to the end of this weekend and I have some good news to tell you.

"It is more going into the last few races knowing that next year is good."

Bearman then dismissed concerns that should an agreement not be reached, Ryo Hirakawa could be drafted in as a ready-made, short notice, replacement, simply saying, "No, it doesn't concern me at all."
